target_customer: Consumers selling or buying used furniture in metro areas, starting in the San Francisco Bay Area
problem: Selling used furniture on Craigslist is slow and risky and buying new is costly. Move Loot picked up, photographed, listed and delivered the furniture.
business_model: Consignment marketplace taking a large cut of the sale price, later shifted toward peer to peer

founders.name: Bill Bobbitt
founders.background_notes: Named co-founder and CEO in the TechCrunch launch article (2014-01-28).

founders.name: Ryan Smith
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page and TechCrunch article. No bio found.

founders.name: Shruti Shah
founders.background_notes: Named in TechCrunch launch article and the 2016 farewell letter.

founders.name: Jenny Karin Morrill
founders.background_notes: Named co-founder in TechCrunch launch article and 2016 farewell letter. YC page lists only Ryan Smith.

exit.reason: Company ceased operations and sold its customer list to Handy. TechCrunch reports it ran out of cash after shifting from consignment to a peer to peer model.

competitors.name: Craigslist
competitors.what: Classifieds where individuals sell used furniture themselves
competitors.traction_then: Default channel for used furniture, per launch coverage

competitors.name: Chairish
competitors.what: Curated marketplace for used furniture with a 20 percent fee
competitors.traction_then: Named in AptDeco coverage as a rival model

competitors.name: AptDeco
competitors.what: Peer to peer used furniture marketplace with bundled delivery in the New York Tri State area, same YC cohort

technical_complexity.rationale: A listing site plus logistics scheduling. The hard parts were operations (pickup, photography, delivery) rather than software.

defensibility.rationale: Consignment logistics were copyable and operationally heavy with no network lock in. AptDeco and Chairish ran similar models.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: AptDeco discussed buying Move Loot assets but nothing came of it (TechCrunch 2016). Handy bought only the customer list.

market_need_then: Moving and used furniture resale were common pain points, and Craigslist was the main channel. Investors funded the model quickly, with about 21 to 22 million dollars raised by late 2015 (TechCrunch 2016, Wikipedia).

identity.visual_style: Playful consumer marketplace with named listings such as Naomi Dining Set (TIME)
identity.voice_and_tone: Casual, with the YC description joking that it is online shopping meets ride sharing meets an ice cream sandwich

branding.brand_signature: Whimsical personified furniture names for each listing
branding.community_and_virality: Covered by TechCrunch, TIME, Business Insider and local TV. Sellers complained publicly after the abrupt shutdown. No merch found.

brand_strength.rationale: Memorable and covered by national press including TIME, but the brand lost trust when sellers were not paid promptly and listings stopped, per TechCrunch 2016.

pivots.from: Consignment model where Move Loot handled pickup and photos
pivots.why: Cost of consignment logistics, as described by TechCrunch (2016)

outcome_analysis: Move Loot raised about 21 to 22 million dollars across a seed in 2014 and a Series A in early 2015 but its consignment logistics were costly. It stopped accepting listings in late May 2016, was reported in sale talks on June 13, and shut down on June 29, 2016, selling only its customer list to Handy. TechCrunch says it ran out of cash after changing to peer to peer, and former employees blamed inexperienced management. AptDeco, same YC cohort and a lighter model, survived.
notes: Seed amount 2.8M comes from a TechCrunch headline seen in search results (June 9, 2014); VentureBeat on April 8, 2014 reported about 2.5M from 15 investors, probably an earlier tranche or the same seed. The July 2015 12.32M figure is a headline of a Form D report cited by Wikipedia and rests on a single source; CB Insights labels July 2015 as Series A II. The three rounds sum above the reported total of 21.8M (Wikipedia, as of Nov 2015) and CB Insights 21.24M, so the rounds overlap or are partly double counted. The seed investors list is taken from the PR Newswire statement that YC and GV were earlier investors. Wikipedia lists the company start as 2013; TechCrunch 2016 says it opened in 2013. The pivot date 2016 is approximate: the source says it pivoted before the shutdown without a date. The brand effect is judged neutral from limited evidence. failure_factors competition_won and unit_economics are judgments from TechCrunch's account and Failory's bad business model label.
